€60 at the Lithuania–Latvia–Belarus border: why euros and zlotys can ruin a trip

The €60 euro-banknote advice at Lithuanian and Latvian borders, EUR and PLN sanctions, why USD differs, EU €10,000 and Belarus $10,000 declarations, red and green lanes.

ComfortLine·Checked 3 November 2026
Important: information only, not an official legal source

For personal information and travel planning only. ComfortLine is not a customs authority. This is not official law, individual legal advice or a border-crossing guarantee. €60 is not a statutory EU-wide cash ceiling. Lithuanian Customs was reported to have applied a €60 euro-banknote personal-use position in 2022; Latvia's current published standard is reasonable personal travel needs without an identical fixed figure. Verify Article 1za of Regulation 765/2006, current national guidance and EAEU declaration requirements before departure.

€60?Historical Lithuanian euro-banknote guidance, not an EU-wide legal ceiling
€10,000EU external-border cash declaration trigger
$10,000Belarus/EAEU cash declaration trigger, strictly above this amount

The traveller who packed everything except the currency rules

Meet Alex, a fictional ComfortLine passenger travelling from Lithuania to Belarus. Passport? Yes. Booking? Yes. Phone battery? Almost. But when he opens his wallet, the customs conversation turns to his euros and Polish zlotys. His original plan was a quick crossing; now someone suggests checking the cash or returning to a currency exchange office in a distant town.

Alex protests: 'I thought only €10,000 had to be declared!' That is precisely the trap. A cash declaration threshold and an EU sanctions restriction on exporting EU-currency banknotes to Belarus are different rules. The scene is imagined; the legal distinction is real. [1] [2]

Why the mysterious €60 keeps appearing

In March 2022 Lithuanian Customs was publicly reported as allowing no more than €60 in euro banknotes per traveller for personal use when travelling to Belarus or Russia. This represents a documented Lithuanian administrative position at that time, not a €60 number written into an EU-wide regulation. Travellers must confirm whether the same interpretation is currently applied at their selected checkpoint. [5]

Latvia's State Revenue Service uses different wording: EU-member-state currency banknotes may be taken to Belarus only in reasonable amounts necessary for personal travel (or for applicable official purposes). Its publicly available explanation does not establish an identical fixed €60 figure. Do not advertise €60 as guaranteed safe—or €61 as an automatic breach everywhere. [4]

Why euros AND Polish zlotys matter, but US dollars differ

Article 1za of EU Regulation 765/2006 restricts supplying or exporting banknotes denominated in any official currency of an EU Member State to Belarus. That includes euro (EUR) banknotes and Polish zloty (PLN) banknotes, not just euros. A narrow exception permits amounts necessary for a traveller's personal use or that of immediate family travelling with them. [1]

The US dollar is not an official EU Member State currency, so the particular denomination-based banknote restriction does not apply to USD banknotes. However, US dollars still count towards EU and EAEU cash-declaration totals, may be subject to source-of-funds controls, and do not provide an opportunity to evade other restrictions. [1] [2]

€10,000: a declaration threshold, not permission to export EU banknotes

People entering or leaving the EU with €10,000 or more in cash or covered equivalent instruments must declare it. A traveller's euro, dollar and zloty notes are aggregated and converted under the applicable exchange rules; the limit is not per currency. Officers can request information or act on smaller amounts when circumstances indicate unlawful activity. [2] [3] [8]

A declaration does not override Article 1za. For instance, carrying €200 in euro banknotes for Belarus can prompt a sanctions question even though it is far below €10,000. Conversely, USD banknotes worth more than €10,000 can trigger the declaration rule without falling into that particular EU-banknote-denomination ban. [1] [2]

Belarus / EAEU: more than $10,000 in either direction

On the Belarus/EAEU side, strictly more than USD 10,000 equivalent in cash and travellers' cheques crossing the customs border in one movement triggers written passenger customs declaration. Aggregate all currencies; declare the entire amount, using the red corridor. When the equivalent exceeds USD 100,000, supporting documents proving the origin of funds are needed. [6] [7]

This is a declaration threshold, not a universal maximum permitted cash amount. Rules of other jurisdictions still apply independently. The EU uses €10,000 or more, whereas the EAEU uses more than $10,000: both the currencies and strictness of the trigger differ. [2] [6]

Outbound and return journeys follow different directions

Lithuania/Latvia → Belarus: on leaving the EU, check Article 1za for EUR/PLN notes and separately the €10,000 EU declaration threshold; on arrival to Belarus, check the over-$10,000 EAEU trigger. Belarus → Lithuania/Latvia: on leaving Belarus, check the over-$10,000 rule, then the €10,000-or-more EU entry declaration. The EU prohibition on banknotes to Belarus does not simply reverse into an identical prohibition on arriving from Belarus. [1] [2] [6]

Do not treat €10,000 and $10,000 as interchangeable numbers. A threshold may be met on one side but not the other after conversion at the official rate applicable on the crossing date. [3] [6]

Green lane, red lane—and the sanctions that neither lane erases

The green corridor is an assertion that nothing requiring declaration is being carried, not a promise against inspection. The red corridor is appropriate when declaration is required. Latvia explicitly directs cash declarants to the red channel where a two-channel system operates; Belarusian Customs directs travellers with over-$10,000 equivalent there as well. [4] [6]

A completed red-lane declaration does not legalize an otherwise prohibited export of EU-currency banknotes. If unsure, ask customs before selecting a corridor or crossing its declaration line. [1] [8]

The currency exchange office is not beside the barrier

In the illustration, Alex is sent back toward the next town's exchange office—far away, of course. This is a satirical scenario, not a factual travel distance for a specific checkpoint. An exchange office may be closed, lack the required currency, or demand identification. Resolve the need for legitimate travel cash and supporting documents before you leave the departure city.

Exchanging money does not remove declaration duties and must not be used to circumvent sanctions. Don't split money among passengers deceptively. Get advice from the relevant customs authority when the legality of your particular cash or purpose is uncertain. [1] [3]

A five-minute checklist beats a five-hour detour

Ask: What banknotes do I have? EUR and PLN are EU-member-state currency notes; USD is not. Whose money is it and what genuine travel use is intended? Is the total at least €10,000 on the EU side or over $10,000 equivalent on the Belarusian side? Which direction and which country am I crossing? [1] [2] [6]

The lesson of Alex's fictional journey: border rules are easiest to understand at the kitchen table, and most expensive to learn at the end of a queue.

Pre-departure cash checklist

  • Check current Lithuanian or Latvian guidance on EUR/PLN banknotes going to Belarus.
  • Do not assume €60 is an EU-wide legal allowance or a guarantee at any checkpoint.
  • Aggregate cash in all currencies for the EU ≥€10,000 declaration trigger.
  • Calculate the Belarus/EAEU >$10,000 trigger separately.
  • Use the red corridor if a declaration is needed and ask before selecting a lane when uncertain.
  • Carry supporting documentation where needed; do not rely on a border-side exchange kiosk.
